# The Three-Day Silence

*A storyline for the product kickoff — what setting up online payments feels like from the other side of the screen.*

---

## Meet Maya

Maya runs a small online store. She is not a developer, not a finance person, not somebody who reads the word "interchange" for fun. She is the kind of owner who packs her own orders, answers her own DMs, and notices — one slow afternoon — that the same thing keeps happening at checkout. A customer fills a cart. A customer gets to the payment screen. A customer asks, *"Wait, you don't take card?"* — and disappears.

She does the math she's been avoiding. Every one of those people was a sale. She had the product, the price, the customer ready to hand over money, and she lost them at the very last step — not because of anything she made, but because of how they could pay for it.[^1]

That is the spark. Card payments stop being a someday-thing. They become a today-thing.

---

## Act One: The Pricing Fog

So Maya opens a dozen browser tabs and goes shopping for a payment provider. This is where the urgency runs straight into a wall.

Every provider's page promises it's the simple one. And every one of them speaks a language she doesn't. Interchange-plus. Flat-rate. Per-transaction. Monthly minimums. She's trying to answer a question any business owner should be able to answer in thirty seconds — *what will this actually cost me?* — and instead she's translating jargon across five tabs that refuse to line up.[^2]

Think of standing in a foreign supermarket where every price tag is in a different currency and none of them convert. You're not being asked to choose. You're being asked to first *learn a system* before you're even allowed to choose. Maya is overwhelmed before she's signed up for anything.

She picks one anyway — not because she's confident, but because she's tired.

---

## Act Two: Handing Over the Keys

Now the provider wants to know who she is. Really know.

EIN. Government-issued ID. Business ownership details. Maya is gathering documents she keeps in a drawer she rarely opens, photographing her own ID, typing in the kind of information you're trained your whole life *not* to type into websites.[^3]

She does it — a little wary, a little careful, double-checking the URL — because she understands the trade. This is the cost of admission. She hands over the most sensitive data she owns in exchange for one thing: the ability to finally get paid.

She hits submit. And then the story stops.

---

## Act Three: The Three-Day Silence

> *This is the part I want the room to sit in.*

Here is what Maya sees after she submits everything: **nothing.**

No progress bar. No "we got your documents." No "expect to hear back by Thursday." No estimate, no checkmark, no human, no signal of any kind. Just a screen, and silence.[^4]

She waits. She refreshes. Same screen. She waits some more.

Put yourself there. You've just handed a stranger your ID, your tax number, your business — and the only thing that comes back is a blank wall. So Maya does what any reasonable person does in a silence that long: **she assumes it's broken.** Not "it's processing." *Broken.* The anxiety she felt handing over her data curdles into doubt, and the doubt has nowhere to go, because nobody is telling her anything.

This wait is **three business days.**[^5] For Maya, with no feedback, three business days is indistinguishable from failure. And this is the make-or-break moment of the entire journey — the point where owners either cross over or quietly walk away. A large share never come back. They don't rage-quit. They just close the tab and conclude this wasn't for them.[^6]

That's the gut-punch I want the team to feel: we very likely lose the most owners *not* at a hard step, but at an empty one. Not because the work was too hard — because the silence was too long.

---

## Act Four: The Payment That Lands

For the owners who *do* hold on, here's the other side.

Three days later — or whenever the silence finally breaks — a real customer reaches Maya's checkout, picks card, and pays. And it just... works. The payment lands. Real money, real customer, no "we don't take card," no apology, no lost sale.[^7]

Relief and pride, in the same breath. The store can take payments now. Maya did the thing. She feels capable.

The only shadow over that ending: how many Mayas never got here — not because they couldn't, but because for three days, nobody told them they were almost home.

---

## What I want us to carry out of this room

One picture. A first-time owner, ID in hand, having handed over everything we asked for, staring at a blank screen for three days, deciding for herself that we're broken.

The whole arc — the pricing fog, the wary handover, the relief at the end — is real. But the moment that decides whether Maya stays or goes is the one where **we say nothing.** The fix isn't a smaller wait. It's *breaking the silence*: a status timeline while she waits, and a proactive ping the second she's verified. Cheap to build. And it sits exactly on the step where we lose the most people.

Let's build the thing that tells Maya she's not alone in the dark.

---

### A note on sourcing

This storyline dramatizes the team's current journey map for first-time online-payments setup. The map records these steps, emotions, and pain points as our working understanding — they are authored from internal knowledge of the flow, **not yet backed by cited research, interviews, or analytics.** The "large share abandon during verification" and "most owners assume it's broken" framing is our hypothesis, not a measured drop-off rate. Treat the verification wait as the highest-conviction *bet* to validate, not a proven number.

[^1]: Research — *realize-need*: sales happening manually; Maya decides she needs a real checkout. (Trigger for the whole journey.)
[^2]: Choose a Provider — *hit-fee-confusion*: fee jargon (interchange, flat-rate, per-transaction) is hard to compare apples-to-apples.
[^3]: Account & Verification — *provide-business-details*: KYC requires EIN, government ID, ownership details.
[^4]: Account & Verification — *connect-bank-account*: verification runs with zero feedback; silence reads as failure.
[^5]: *connect-bank-account*: duration / wait time of 3 business days with no status feedback.
[^6]: *connect-bank-account*: `momentOfTruth` — the single biggest drop-off; failure mode is owners concluding it's broken and giving up. (Hypothesis — not a measured rate.)
[^7]: Test & Go Live — *first-real-sale* / *first-payout*: first live payment lands; relief and pride.
